title: Threads: The Half Written Value Nobody Sees Coming

questions.question: Two threads access the same memory, one of them writing, with no synchronisation. What is that?
options: A data race, which is undefined behaviour rather than merely a stale value
A race condition that at worst gives a slightly old reading
Safe, as long as the value is a single variable
A deadlock
questions.explanation: The distinction matters because it licenses the compiler to assume it cannot happen, and to keep the value in a register so a thread never sees the other's write at all.

questions.question: Why can a pose be seen half written?
options: Three doubles are three separate stores, and a reader can arrive between any two
Because doubles are not aligned
Because the compiler reorders the fields
Because a pose is passed by reference
questions.explanation: The value assembled from two different writes describes a position the robot was never in, which is worse than a stale reading.

questions.question: Does volatile fix sharing between threads?
options: No. It stops the compiler eliding accesses but gives no atomicity and no ordering
Yes, that is exactly what it is for
Yes, but only for single variables
Only when combined with a mutex
questions.explanation: It is the most common wrong fix in robotics code, inherited from embedded C where it means something different. A volatile pose still tears.

questions.question: Why must the read take the lock as well as the write?
options: One unguarded reader is enough to bring the tearing straight back
Reads are slower than writes
Because lock_guard requires it
It does not, only writers need to lock
questions.explanation: A mutex only helps when every access takes it. Guarding half the accesses guards nothing.

questions.question: Two of this lesson's tests failed against the unsynchronised code five times out of five, and two failed zero times out of five. What does that show?
options: A race that does not reproduce is still a race, so testing alone cannot find them
The last two tests are wrong and should be deleted
The unsynchronised code is correct for those two cases
Races only happen under heavy load
questions.explanation: Both undetected races were genuinely present, and the thread sanitizer reported them immediately. It will reproduce on the robot, at temperature, in front of a customer.

questions.question: Why is a mutex the wrong tool on a path with a deadline?
options: A thread that cannot take the lock waits for as long as the holder takes, which is unbounded
Mutexes are slow in absolute terms
Mutexes cannot be used from more than two threads
Because they require dynamic allocation
questions.explanation: The worst case is what a deadline cares about, and priority inversion makes it worse: a low priority thread holding a lock can block a high priority one.
